content: Ancylostomiasis is a hookworm infection caused by soil-transmitted helminths (STH). It predominantly occurs in tropical and subtropical regions of the world, particularly in countries with low socioeconomic status. The common symptoms of ancylostomiasis include anorexia, flatulence, diarrhea, weight loss, pallor, dyspnea, weakness, generalized edema, melena, hematemesis, dizziness, syncope, cough, sneezing, hemoptysis, nausea, vomiting, pharyngeal irritation, and itchy, erythematous, serpiginous skin lesions. The primary treatment for ancylostomiasis involves anti-helminthic therapies. These medications are recommended for patients diagnosed with the infection. Ancylostomiasis was first identified in 1838 by an Italian physician named Dubini. The infection can be classified into two groups based on the species of hookworm: human hookworms (Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus) and zoonotic hookworms (Ancylostoma braziliense, Ancylostoma caninum, Ancylostoma ceylanicum, and Uncinaria stenocephala). The pathophysiology of ancylostomiasis involves the life cycle of hookworms. Mature female hookworms release eggs in the host’s small intestine, which are then excreted in feces. Under suitable conditions, these eggs hatch in the soil and develop into infective filariform larvae (L3 stage). These larvae can enter the human body through the skin or oral ingestion. Once inside, they travel through the bloodstream to the lungs, migrate across the alveoli, ascend the bronchial tree to the pharynx, and eventually reach the small intestine. There, they mature into blood-feeding adult worms. The most common causes of ancylostomiasis are Ancylostoma duodenale, Necator americanus, and Ancylostoma ceylanicum. Less common organisms include Ancylostoma braziliense, Ancylostoma caninum, and Uncinaria stenocephala. Ancylostomiasis must be differentiated from other diseases with similar manifestations. For cutaneous symptoms, it should be distinguished from contact dermatitis, scabies, migratory myiasis, and cercarial dermatitis. For gastrointestinal bleeding, it should be differentiated from conditions such as portal hypertension, Meckel’s diverticulum, inflammatory bowel disease, NSAID-induced small bowel disease, angiectasias, adenocarcinoma, leiomyoma, and lymphoma. The global prevalence of ancylostomiasis is approximately 1 billion people. It affects individuals of all ages but is more common in children and women of childbearing age. The mortality rate due to hookworm infections in tropical regions is estimated to be 50,000–60,000 deaths per year. Men are more frequently affected than women. Risk factors for ancylostomiasis include exposure to soil containing infective filariform larvae, poor sanitation, low socioeconomic status, and limited educational attainment. Most individuals with ancylostomiasis remain asymptomatic. Symptoms typically develop through direct skin contact with contaminated soil or via the fecal-oral route. Common complications include iron deficiency anemia, intellectual and cognitive developmental issues in children, and severe anemia, impaired growth, premature birth, and neonatal anemia in pregnant women. With appropriate treatment, the prognosis is generally excellent. The diagnostic test of choice for ancylostomiasis is the microscopic detection of hookworm eggs in stool samples. Most patients are asymptomatic, but common symptoms include anorexia, flatulence, diarrhea, weight loss, pallor, dyspnea, weakness, generalized edema, melena, hematemesis, dizziness, syncope, cough, sneezing, hemoptysis, nausea, vomiting, pharyngeal irritation, and itchy, erythematous, serpiginous skin lesions. Physical examination findings may include pallor, fatigue, dizziness, serpiginous and erythematous skin lesions, palpable plaques associated with edema, and abdominal distension. Laboratory findings often reveal decreased hemoglobin levels, eosinophilia, and the presence of live, motile worms during upper gastrointestinal endoscopy. There are no specific findings on X-rays or CT scans associated with ancylostomiasis. However, upper gastrointestinal endoscopy can demonstrate live and motile worms in the gastrointestinal tract. Treatment primarily involves anti-helminthic medications. The efficacy of treatment depends on the severity of the infection, geographical distribution, and the patient’s age. In severe cases, blood transfusions and iron supplements may be necessary. Surgical intervention is not recommended for managing ancylostomiasis. Primary prevention strategies include periodic mass anthelmintic treatment for at-risk populations, avoiding barefoot gardening, and educating patients on proper hygiene and sanitation practices.
